ECD vs flow rate

At the casing shoe and at the bit, against the FIT. The dots mark the current flow rate.

Table view

Section by section

Annular sections from surface to bit, then the pipe, bit and surface losses.

Pressure vs pipe speed

Surge running in (felt at the weak zone) and swab pulling out (felt at the bottom), against the limits you set.

Table view

Speed card for the floor

Average speed, time per 40 ft joint and the pressure each speed puts on the hole.

Drill pipe pressure while the kill mud goes down

Hold these pressures as the strokes count up. Kill mud gains its hydrostatic where the well drops in TVD, so on a deviated or horizontal well the pressure falls faster through the vertical and the curve and hardly moves in the lateral. The dashed line is the even step-down of a vertical-well kill sheet.

Kill schedule

Step by step

Volumes and strokes

String and annulus from the well and string on the left, at the kill pump’s output and rate.

Kick tolerance from here to section TD

The biggest gas kick you can shut in and circulate out without breaking down the shoe, as the bit goes deeper with this mud weight. The lower line sets it.

Table view

Volumetric bleed schedule

Lubricate and bleed

Slow pump rates

The newest SPR for each pump and rate in the log, checked against the current mud weight, bit depth and time. ▶ marks the one the kill sheet uses.

Hole fill against the steel

Expected against actual from the trip tank readings on the left. Pulling out, actual falling below expected means the hole is taking less than the steel coming out.

Trip sheet

Flowback fingerprint

Flowback after the pumps stop on each connection, against the well’s normal ones.

Hook load while running

Expected weight indicator readings as the shoe goes down, from the surveys and your friction factors, with the readings you log on top.

Table view

Centralizers

Spacing that holds your standoff against the casing’s side load, joint by joint through the open hole.

Tally

Joint by joint from the shoe up. “Shoe at” is where the shoe will be once that joint is in.

Cumulative cost against the AFE

Spread, tickets, rentals and mud by day, the AFE as a straight line to its last day, and the estimate at completion where the projection ends.

Vendors

Orders
Every request to a vendor (services, trucks, products and rentals) from the alert to the finished job. Red is waiting on the vendor, yellow is under way, green is done.

Call list

Trucks
Every load to move for the jobs ahead, with the time it has to be on location.

Predicted from the depth now, the progress rate and the casing program. Set a time when you know it; the steps after it move with it.

Pressure to hold while you displace
The pressure the pumps must hold as the fluids move, from the first barrel of spacer to the plug bump. Below zero, the cement is free-falling faster than you pump.

Buckling limits by inclination
Compression the pipe can take before it buckles, against the compression you put on it. Above the sinusoidal line the pipe snakes; above the helical line it coils, drag climbs fast and weight stops reaching the bit.

Mud cost per foot by depth
Mud cost to date over the feet drilled, at each report, against the offsets at the same depth and the mud program’s budget.

      
Mud cost to date by depth
What the mud had cost by each depth on this well and on the offsets. Lower is cheaper to the same depth.

      
By interval
Each interval on the reports, its cost per foot, the offsets’ cost over the same depths and the budget.

      
Lost circulation events
Built from the reports’ downhole losses: where, how much, the LCM it took and how long to cure.

      
LCM used
Every LCM product on the reports, split between loss events and background treatment.

Calculator: standard oilfield field-unit formulas (API RP 13B/13D conventions where they apply). Models: Bingham plastic (the annular method most mud-reporting software uses) and API RP 13D Herschel-Bulkley; Moore slip velocity; Robinson CCI; Burkhardt surge with clinging constant. Estimates for planning. Trust PWD, MPD and the rig's gauges over any model, and agree weight and rate changes with the company man.
